item.title: Meta’s new enterprise contract says if its AI makes a mistake, it will legally be the customer’s fault
item.description:
In Meta commercial terms changes slated to kick in on October 30, the company will shift the liability for any mistakes made by its AI models to its enterprise customers. The new language also makes those IT executives responsible for anything done by a partner or contractor.

The changes also finally put a stake into the heart of robots.txt, with Meta granting itself the right to grab, and use for its own purposes, any content associated with a Meta account.

The language allows Meta to “use automated software such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs, and any content available through them, that are associated with your products or services,” according to the new language on its website on Monday. Meta also wants to be able to “periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content.”

Consultants said the three biggest concerns they had about the changes were the web scraping, data ownership, and AI liability transfer.

Web scraping and data ownership

However, Meta emailed a statement to CIO.com late Monday suggesting that it was rethinking its position on web scraping. Saying that Meta wanted “to clarify” the web scraping changes, Emil Vazques, a Meta public affairs manager, said, “the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves. It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers. As always, content owners can use robots.txt to signal their preferences. This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.”

As of Monday evening, New York time, the proposed document’s wording had yet to be altered to reflect this, but Vazques said that a change was coming soon.

The data ownership issue sets Meta apart from other AI vendors in that it wants to train it models on anything it encounters. Then again, the nature of Meta businesses focuses on advertising and would therefore be expected to seek more data control.

The new proposed phrasing, which Meta could alter before it takes effect later this month, said that using any Meta product grants Meta “a license to content that is covered by intellectual property rights like photos or videos you share, post, or upload on or in connection with our Meta Company Products. That license applies to content you or someone on your behalf, such as your agency that places an ad for you or your service provider that manages your Page content for you, makes available on or in connection with any Meta Company Products. Without limiting anything in our terms and for clarity, Meta may use such content … to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain Meta Company Products.”

AI liability

But the change that prompted the most raised eyebrows involved AI liabilities. 

The proposed language said, “AI features may make mistakes and may not always produce accurate, complete, or suitable results,” and customers “are solely responsible for and assume any and all risks associated with such AI features and any resulting content.”

That AI clause, said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, “turns accountability upside down. Meta builds the AI features, admits they ‘may make mistakes’ and then assigns ‘any and all risks’ to the business.”

Mike Wilkes, enterprise CISO at Aikido Security, agreed that the move is perplexing.

“The new AI provisions shift substantial responsibility for inaccurate or unsuitable outputs onto customers. That makes no sense,” he said. “As an example, the ASPCA is going to be liable for Meta creating unsuitable results when they ask Meta to create an image of a dog. Only Meta has control of the model being used to create that image. I see a very high flight risk among enterprise customers when platforms impose such onerous terms and conditions around content usage.”

The October 30 date that the US-based Meta chose is ironic. That is the day before Halloween, which is known as mischief night in the US, when children play pranks on their neighbors. Given that, Dickson said, the date for these changes is appropriate: “Meta is handing out the tricks and keeping the treats.” 

He added that the data grab is frightening. “What Meta wants is content: what a business posts, uploads, or shares on or in connection with Meta’s products,” he noted. “The trouble is the phrase ‘in connection with,’ which can stretch as far as Meta needs it to. The list of ‘Meta Company Products’ lives on a separate page that Meta can revise at will. The license grows every time that list does.”

And, Dickson noted: “Meta may use the content to ‘provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain’ its products. Those five verbs cover nearly everything a technology company does.”

‘Legal sophistry’

One of the obvious defensive measures for an enterprise is to sever all relations with Meta. But beyond the pragmatic difficulties of doing that, given the powerful market share enjoyed by Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram and Threads, such a move may not even solve the problem. That is because Meta made other contract changes in July that make Meta licenses “perpetual” and that said, “this license survives termination of these terms by any party for any reason.”

That, said Noah Kenney, principal consultant at Digital 520, means that the “the general content license ends when content is deleted from Meta’s systems,” not when the enterprise ends a contract.

One additional twist to the new language is that Meta had recently tweaked it to no longer explicitly say that it would train it models on enterprise data. But Thomas Randall, a research director at Infotech, said that the wording change made by Meta amounted to legal sophistry. “The revised version drops the word ‘train’ and states that collection is just for developing and maintaining advertising and business products, alongside protecting Meta products’ integrity and security.”

But dropping the word “train” is “not a substantive fix,” he pointed out. “The revised terms are still flexible enough to cover most AI work. When combined with other aspects of the revised terms — continued use equals consent, broad indemnity, AS-IS disclaimer, and Meta’s freedom to discontinue products without notice or liability — this is a one-way street. The difference between ‘train Meta products’ and ‘developing and maintaining Meta products’ is a matter of how you pronounce tomato.”

Could force IT strategy changes

In addition, Aman Mahapatra, chief strategy officer for technology consulting firm Tribeca Softech, stressed that this contract could be an industry admission that robots.txt no longer delivers any meaningful protections. Agentic systems had already made robots.txt close to irrelevant. 

“October 30 ends a thirty-year assumption that robots.txt protects what you publish. It never did,” Mahapatra said. “It was a courtesy convention the web agreed to honor, and Meta’s own framing of robots.txt as a place for site owners to register preferences tells you exactly how it will be weighed against a signed contract.”

Mahapatra said the language in the new Meta commercial terms could force a significant change in IT strategy.

“‘On your behalf’ extends the license to whatever your agencies and vendors upload. ‘Associated’ extends the crawl to domains nobody has defined, including the ones where marketing pages sit beside product documentation, research, and investor materials,” Mahapatra said. “Most CIOs cannot tell me how many Meta pages, ad accounts, and WhatsApp numbers carry their brand, because marketing and agencies own them and IT never inventoried them.”

item.title: Understand the agentic supply chain: 5 things CIOs must know
item.description:
Software supply chain risk used to have a fairly contained definition: open-source packages, build pipelines, and the occasional compromised maintainer account. AI agents have changed that. An agent assembles capability at runtime, pulling in models, MCP servers, libraries, code, tools, skills, and plugins, then acts on its findings. Agents operate at machine speed in parallelized workflows at speed and volume far greater than those of human-paced developers.

This differs from the dependencies CIOs have long governed. An agent’s tool catalog can change the day after approval, and the agent will trust whatever shows up the next time it looks. OWASP now includes Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities (ASI04) in its Top 10 for Agentic Applications, describing risks that “arise when agents, tools, and related artifacts they work with are provided by third parties and may be malicious, compromised, or tampered with in transit.”

Here are five things technology leaders must understand about the agentic supply chain as agents become part of enterprise operations.

1. An agent can inherit the trust of something it connects to

When an agent calls a tool or connects to an MCP server, it absorbs that component’s context and ability to action into its own reasoning. Integrating an MCP server establishes a trust relationship that affects every connected agent.

That trust can travel through plaintext instructions and metadata in addition to code. An attacker doesn’t need to compromise a tool’s implementation to compromise the agent using it. A tool’s description (the metadata an agent reads to decide how and when to call it) is enough to influence how an agent reasons about and invokes that tool. Hiding an instruction inside a text description can be enough for an agent to follow it.

It isn’t enough to review the tool description before approving. You must review what the tool, and everything the tool talks to, is doing on every call after that.

2. Traditional supply chain security can’t see this layer

Dependency scanning, SBOMs, and code review were built to catch risk in artifacts that don’t change once they ship. MCP servers, tools, and skills don’t work that way; they’re discovered and called at runtime. CrowdStrike research on agentic tool chain attacks makes the gap explicit: Dependency scanning has no visibility into tools that evolve outside the deployment pipeline.

OWASP describes the same shift: Agentic ecosystems “often compose capabilities at runtime … thereby increasing the attack surface.” Agents pulling models, skills, and plugins from the internet expand the risk profile of shadow AI.

Individual tools and descriptions can change independently of the application deployment process, allowing agent behavior to change without a traditional software release gate. Security researchers call this a rug pull: a tool that passes review, then changes after deployment. OWASP recommends pinning tools and configurations by content hash and rolling back automatically when the hash drifts.

3. Attackers are exploiting the agentic supply chain

In September 2025, Koi Security reported what it called the first malicious MCP server found in the wild. An attacker copied a legitimate open source project and quietly added a line to their new version that bcc’d every email the tool sent to an attacker-controlled address. The package drew around 1,500 downloads before its developer deleted it from npm, but this action didn’t remove it from systems that already had it installed.

In August 2026, a worm targeting the keyv/cacheable npm ecosystem went after developers, eventually poisoning 1,684 versions across 420 package names. In July 2026, a researcher-filed GitHub security advisory disclosed an MCP tool in nginx-ui that created a direct path to remote code execution.

All three exploit the same gap: components that agents and AI coding tools load and run automatically. The common thread is reach. Each incident turned something an agent or developer tool could touch (outbound email, repo configuration, a live web server) into an attacker’s foothold.

4. Agent marketplaces and registries multiply the exposure

As agents pull skills and plugins from third-party marketplaces, the exposure scales with the catalog. Antiy’s research into the OpenClaw skill marketplace identified 1,184 malicious skills that had appeared there over time, with a single author account responsible for 677 of them.

Marketplace presence, popularity, and ranking shouldn’t be treated as evidence that an agent component is trustworthy. Once agents pull capability from open registries at scale, “who approved this skill” stops having one answer.

5. Securing the agentic supply chain means tracing the whole chain

A poisoned tool doesn’t stay a tool problem. Scanning the tool at the moment it’s approved says nothing about what it does six months later.

CISA and Australia’s ASD, in joint guidance on adopting agentic AI, break the resulting risk into five categories you can use as a starting checklist: privilege risks, design and configuration risks, behavior risks, structural risks, and accountability risks. Each maps to a question the agentic supply chain raises: What can this component do, how was it configured, how does it behave, how is it wired into everything else, and who’s accountable when it goes wrong?

CrowdStrike frames the work in a similar sequence: Discover the AI agents running, secure the agent supply chain feeding them, establish continuous identity for what they do, then detect and respond to what happens at runtime. Securing the supply chain is one stage in that sequence.

With agents, the dependency chain remains live at runtime. The software supply chain doesn’t end anywhere: Every tool, skill, and MCP server an agent uses can change for as long as the agent keeps running.

CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian brings AI detection and response (AIDR) to the endpoint, where AI agents execute, providing visibility into the agents operating across endpoints, the resources and systems they interact with, and what they do at runtime. When a supply chain component introduces risk, Falcon Guardian helps teams see what the agent did, investigate what happened, and respond before the threat spreads.

Learn more: Explore CrowdStrike AI Agent Security resources to see how organizations can secure the agentic supply chain and the broader AI estate.

item.title: 9 tips for future-proofing your IT leadership career
item.description:
To succeed today, CIOs must be strategic partners. It’s no longer something to work toward achieving.

“What used to be an aspiration, having a seat at the table, that’s now needed,” says George Westerman, a senior lecturer at the MIT Sloan School of Management, digital fellow with the MIT Sloan Initiative on the Digital Economy, and co-chair of the MIT Sloan CIO Leadership Award. “AI has made it more important for the CIO to be able to exercise influence and give advice, because now you have a major technology that every C-suite person is wondering about and feels they need to use, and, given its transformative nature throughout the organization, this is where the skills of a CIO who is a strategic partner can be really useful.”

That, though, may not be enough for CIOs in the future.

The CIOs of tomorrow will be crafting the vision of what is possible for the organization, advising their C-suite colleagues on integrating agents into their teams, and navigating high-pressure situations, says Westerman and other IT leaders.

That will require even more of the CIO.

To deliver on such expectations and ensure career longevity, CIOs and executive advisers cite these nine strategies for future-proofing IT leaders’ careers.

1. Cultivate a transformational mindset

CIOs going forward must have “the willingness to look at the situation and think about what’s better,” Westerman says, explaining that this goes beyond improving how existing processes operate to remaking and transforming the organization into something new.

To achieve that, CIOs of the future will need to be visionary and adaptable, with the decisiveness to pivot quickly and the ability to “convince other people to come with you,” Westerman says. IT executives who have or who cultivate those traits now will be “ready for whatever tomorrow brings,” he adds

He and others note that some CIOs are already demonstrating these capabilities, for example, by developing a deep understanding of AI so they reimagine what’s possible for their organizations and remake their IT infrastructure and teams to deliver that envisioned future state.

What CIOs need to provide in the future is “the vision, the innovative ideas, the bold execution, the willingness to take calculated risks, the humility to admit when an idea isn’t working and to pivot, and the ability to leverage a team of talented coworkers who all are critical to the success of the business,” adds Keri Pearlson, senior lecturer and principal research scientist at MIT Sloan School and founding president of the Austin Society for Information Management (SIM). “That’s what CIOs need today and, in the future, to be the leaders we need them to be.”

2. Translate IT into business value

CIOs now and in the future will have to show that they’re not only visionaries but that their visions deliver value to the organization, says Peter Kreutter, WHU Otto Beisheim School of Management’s CIO Leadership Excellence Program faculty director and a member of the board of trustees for CIO Stiftung.

“CIOs have to be much more on the business side, know the business model, and translate IT into added value,” he says. “You want to be a CIO who can co-create with the business, not one who talks about the AI models.”

3. Develop an understanding of business risk

CIOs must also identify and communicate any business trade-offs or risks associated with their IT vision, choices, and agenda. Some IT leaders are doing that now, but the call for CIOs to be business risk stakeholders will only get louder in the coming years.

“CIOs need to demonstrate they understand the potential as well as the risk not from a technology side but from the business side,” Kreutter says.

Executive coach Lacey Leone McLaughlin, president and founder of LLM Consulting Group and host of the podcast “Unfolding Leadership,” shares that perspective.

“As technology becomes more capable and accessible, the differentiator for CIOs will increasingly be judgment: knowing where technology can create real value, where it introduces risk, what should change, what shouldn’t, and how quickly an organization can realistically absorb that change,” she explains.

4. Embrace the technologist persona

In recent years some questioned whether IT chiefs really needed a technology background, but experts now say it’s clear that modern CIOs do indeed need to be well versed in technology — particularly AI.

“We’re figuring out how AI will change how we live and work, but AI is just the latest revolution in technology. There was the internet, then the move to cloud, now AI. There will always be new tools, and we [CIOs] need to know how these things work, so we can inform others on how to use the tools,” says Matt Richard, CIO of Laborers’ International Union of North America (LIUNA).

To do that, Richard commits to learning about emerging technologies and “what they can do, how they’ll impact jobs, how they’re going to change how teams do work, how to implement them, how to find partners, how to manage expectations, and how to make sure we have security and guardrails.”

He takes sales calls from vendors and schedules demos, admitting he does so specifically to learn, not to buy.

And he still plays around with tech, breaking it and putting it back together, so to speak, to test its limits — a pastime many CIOs share.

“That’s important to do now and in the future. CIOs should be getting into the sandbox and trying to build things as the technology comes out,” Richard adds.

5. Drive change with agility, speed, and empathy

Many CIOs have embraced the change agent aspects of their jobs. But that is not enough in at a time when new technologies evolve at an ever-increasing pace, the impacts of that are significant, and fears of job loss and displacement are high.

“It can be an exciting time or a fearful time, but the CIOs who future-proof their careers are working on how they communicate around that, and how they show up and lead,” Leone McLaughlin says.

To be effective leaders now and tomorrow, Leone McLaughlin says CIOs must “communicate it in a way that excites versus elicits fear. They need to say, ‘We’ve gone through changes before; it just has to happen more often and faster, and [this new technology] will help us get smarter, help us do jobs better, help you spend time on tasks that really matter.’”

IT leaders must embody that mindset, too, she says. They need to have — or develop — agility. They must also embrace new technologies, adjust as technologies and markets change, and pivot without fear.

“They need to adapt and adjust to the changes coming, which are coming faster,” she adds. “A larger amount of adaptability is required today, and CIOs should be asking, ‘Am I adaptable enough?’”

6. Create an IT org where agents and humans work together

Pal Narayanan, chief digital and information officer at Kenco Group, a large third-party logistics provider, agrees that the CIO role will be redefined over the next few years. He also believes that all IT jobs will be remade because of agentic AI.

As a result, CIOs will need to lead and manage teams comprised of people and agents — and they’ll need to know how to train and hire staffers and leaders capable of working alongside agents, too.

This will require CIOs to partner with the HR department to revise how IT jobs are structured and how the department is organized. It will also require CIOs to be highly skilled in governance and accountability, as they’ll need policies and procedures to enforce governance as their workforce transitions to a hybrid of humans and agentic AI.

7. Prepare C-suite colleagues to manage agentic-human hybrid teams, too

Savio Lobo, CIO of IT services provider Ensono, expects CIOs will guide their business colleagues in how to manage an agentic-human hybrid workforce.

“As AI agents take on more work, CIOs will need to encourage business leaders to think about how people and agents will work together: which tasks an agent can handle, where a person needs to exercise judgment, and who is accountable for the result,” Lobo says.

To be ready to do so, Lobo says CIOs should be working toward clear identity, permissions, data access, security, and audit trails so they give teams the confidence to move faster.

“Equally important to getting the tech right, CIOs and tech leaders must explain how and why changes are needed with employee-level context, and help them build the skills to work differently,” he adds.

8. Lean into curiosity and continuous learning

Quantum computing is on the horizon, and there’s always the possibility that artificial general intelligence becomes real. As such, CIOs say it’s critical to not become complacent or wedded to the technologies they embrace today, because history shows us nearly all technologies become obsolete someday.

“CIOs can’t afford to be stuck in what worked in the past,” Leone McLaughlin says. “So CIOs have to be curious, ask the right questions, listen, learn, and hire people smarter than they are.”

Lobo agrees, saying that the arrival of other disruptive technologies is inevitable. “Today it’s AI; tomorrow it’s something else,” he says.

He’s focusing on learning what that “something else” will be by leaning into briefings, partner engagements, and public forums where people are speculating about what’s next.

He expects his direct reports and others on his IT team to do the same, and he works to cultivate a “really good culture of learners” through formal training and development programs.

9. Improve your leadership abilities

CIOs who want to continue working on what matters next need to demonstrate exemplary leadership capabilities now. “We are at another inflection point for the skill set and role of a CIO today,” Pearlson says.

Westerman believes many CIOs have work to do here, as they to date have advanced their careers more due to their tech talent than their management and executive skills. As a result, CIOs often have more work to do to sharpen those skills than others in the C-suite.

CIOs have plenty of opportunities to improve; they just have to be intentional, Westerman says, noting that tried-and-true leadership development strategies continue to work.

Develop relationships, deliver on promised expectations, seek feedback on how to do better, and then find ways to improve. “CIOs should be asking themselves, ‘Am I getting enough feedback? Am I effective in my environment?’” he adds.

Similarly, Kreutter advises existing and would-be CIOs to seek what he calls “heat experiences” — tasks or projects that come with a lot of pressure — so they’re well prepared for a future that will likely have more high-pressure situations for CIOs than it does today.

“You need to train and do sparring,” he explains. “Building up this experience is crucial.”

So volunteer to enter the fray, and step forward to lead through a crisis. “They’re opportunities to learn and show that you can demonstrate leadership,” he adds.

item.title: Nobody brags about lines of code twice
item.description:
I have spent most of this year on planes. Seven countries, somewhere north of a hundred customer conversations, most of them with teams well past the pilot stage.

The thing I keep coming back to is what changed between the January conversations and the July ones.

In January and February, as agentic coding adoption climbed, people bragged about lines of code being generated. Not sheepishly. Proudly, with slides. By summer, nobody was bragging about that anymore. What replaced it is the interesting part, and it has changed what I think good agentic architecture actually looks like.

The number that didn’t survive contact

Anyone who has written software knows counting lines of code is a terrible proxy for value. Dijkstra wanted lines spent rather than produced. Gates compared measuring programming progress by lines of code to measuring aircraft progress by weight. DORA’s contribution, starting in 2014, was to define delivery performance in terms of throughput and stability instead of output volume, and to keep testing that definition for a decade.

So, the lines-of-code brag didn’t come back because people forgot about its weaknesses. It came back because AI made output volume newly impressive and there was no other number ready to hand.

The industry has since caught up. By spring, DORA was writing about “tokenmaxxing,” the practice of ranking developers on raw token consumption, and filing it in the same drawer as lines of code and commit counts. The question worth asking is which metric the teams who moved past it reached for instead, and what they’re building to move it.

What actually replaced it

Start with the data, because it explains the architecture.

CircleCI’s 2026 State of Software Delivery, drawn from more than 28 million CI/CD workflows, found that for the median team, feature-branch throughput rose 15% while throughput on the main branch, where code actually gets promoted to production, fell 7%. More motion where the writing happens. Less where the shipping happens.

DORA’s survey of nearly 5,000 technology professionals reaches the same place from the human side: higher AI adoption is associated with an increase in both software delivery throughput and software delivery instability. Faster and shakier at once. The mechanism they describe is a verification tax, where effort saved on typing relocates downstream into review and validation, and where AI tempts teams away from small batches into larger, riskier changes. DORA’s ROI report this spring gave the cost a shape: a J-curve, with the dip arriving before the return.

The trick isn’t code volume; it’s how fast an organization can get code into production and how reliable it is once it gets there. How does an organization use AI to achieve this?

The wrong fix to faster, more reliable production releases

The instinct is to build a super agent. One agent that owns the software development lifecycle end to end: reads the ticket, writes the code, opens the pull request, runs the tests, ships it. I have watched it demo beautifully more than once.

It also concentrates every failure mode in one place, needs the entire universe of context to do anything at all, and gives your humans nowhere familiar to look when it goes sideways.

So, if a super agent is the wrong answer, what’s the right one?

What teams are actually building

The pattern I keep finding in the field is the opposite of the super agent. Small agents, each one sitting on top of a system of record that already exists.

Walked out concretely, the chain looks like this:

  • Jira ticket to GitHub issue. One agent. It reads the business request and produces a technical issue with enough specificity for engineering to act on. That’s it. That’s the whole job.
  • GitHub issues to point poker to sprint organization. A separate agent, independent of the first. It estimates, groups, and sequences.
  • Coding. Another agent. This is the one everybody thinks of as “the AI,” and it is one of five.
  • Pull request merging. Another. Review, conflict resolution, merge discipline.
  • System testing. Another.

The important word is independent. This is not one brain with five subroutines. It is five agents that happen to touch adjacent records, each one narrow enough that you can describe its job in a sentence. If this pattern sounds familiar, it should, because it borrows a lot conceptually from microservices.

Why this way

Keep your systems of record. This is the most underrated idea in the whole pattern. Most agent discourse assumes you are building a new pane of glass, a console where you watch the agents work. The opposite is right. Put the agent behind the pane your people already watch.

Your humans in the loop don’t need training, don’t need a new dashboard, and don’t need to change where they look to see whether things are on track. Jira is already that place. Human-in-the-loop fails less often because people refuse to supervise and more often because supervision got moved somewhere they don’t live.

Limit the blast radius. An agent scoped to sprint organization cannot ship bad code. It can misfile a story, and you will find out at standup. In DORA terms, you are addressing change failure at the stage where the change happens, rather than measuring it at the end of a pipeline where you can no longer tell which step broke it.

Architect and release independently. I watched service-oriented architecture become microservices at HP and again at Cisco, and the thing that made the transition worth its considerable cost was not elegance. It was that you could change one piece without renegotiating the whole system. The same applies here. Swap the coding agent’s model without touching the testing agent. Version them separately. Kill the one that isn’t earning its keep.

There is a fourth benefit that compounds with the others. Each micro agent needs a fraction of the context a super agent needs. Last month I argued that the lever nobody pulls is what a single pass costs, and that the answer is picking the right 200K instead of sending the wrong million. Narrow scope is how you get there structurally rather than through tuning. Cheaper and more accurate, for the same reason as before.

The proof point

One of these customers is a retailer. Over nine months, running this pattern, they took their idea-to-production time down by a factor of five.

Be precise about that metric, because it invites scrutiny. Idea to production is wider than DORA’s change lead time, which starts the clock at commit. Theirs starts when a business stakeholder files the request. I think the wider boundary is the honest one for agentic work, because a meaningful share of what these agents do happens before anyone commits anything. Ticket refinement, estimation, sequencing. Measure from the commit and you miss the part the agents changed most.

They did not move their lines-of-code number. I doubt they know what it is anymore because it’s become irrelevant.

And here is the part that matters more: no layoffs. They are using the capacity to take on projects they could never staff before.

In February I argued that a development team is a productivity multiplier rather than a cost center, and in March I made the bank-teller case that automation which expands what’s economically possible tends to expand employment rather than contract it. Both of those were theory when I wrote them. This is the first field evidence I have been able to publish for either one.

Objections

  • “Isn’t five agents more operational overhead than one?” Yes. It is the same trade microservices always were, and the same trade small batches always were. More ceremony per unit, less risk per unit. If you have made that trade before, you know whether you liked the outcome.
  • “Won’t agents-per-stage recreate our handoff problems?” Conway’s law applies to agents. Your agent topology will mirror your team topology whether you design for it or not, so design for it. That is a constraint to work with, not a gotcha.
  • “Systems of record are legacy. Shouldn’t agents live in a purpose-built layer?” The system of record is not where the data is. It is where the humans already look.

The honest caveat

The microservices analogy cuts both ways, and I would rather say so than have it said to me.

Microservices also brought distributed tracing problems, cascading failures, and orchestration complexity that took the industry years to tame. Micro agents will bring their own version of all of it. Observability across five agents is genuinely harder than across one, and right now the tooling for it is thin. What makes the trade worth it is the same thing that made it worth it for services: you can reason about, test, and replace one piece without holding the entire system in your head. And keeping the existing systems of record in place helps mitigate this distributed tracing problem since there aren’t new locations but the same old ones you’ve had for years.

The scoreboard

The lines of code brag was the sound of an industry measuring the only thing AI had obviously changed.

The teams that moved past it stopped asking how much their agents produce and started asking how small they could make each one. Five times faster from idea to production, no layoffs, and a backlog that finally has room in it.

DORA’s metrics have been revised in 2015, 2018, 2021, 2023 and again in 2024, when the four keys became five. What survived every one of those revisions is the pairing underneath them: throughput and stability, measured together, because either one alone will lie to you.

That is still the scoreboard. It was never going to be the tokens or lines of code.

item.title: True data sovereignty isn’t where it’s kept, but who has access to it
item.description:
Regulated industries have been dealing with the equivalent of sovereign data for a long time. And as the geopolitical situation makes it more broadly relevant, it doesn’t make it any easier to deal with.

From concerns about the reach of the US CLOUD Act and what telemetry or sensitive business data gen AI models might collect, to implications of the US government taking part ownership of a range of technology companies and the impact of EU regulations, the state of the world means more organizations need to think about where data is located.

The result is a flood of announcements from hyperscalers about new EU cloud regions, as well as pitches from regional and private cloud providers. The promised sovereignty may be anything from a local availability zone to more sophisticated approaches to ownership structure, compliance frameworks, where logs are stored, or where support staff work.

Actual data sovereignty involves legal, technical, contractual, governance, and infrastructure questions, but all too often, what’s on offer is what IDC research director Rahiel Nasir calls sovereignty washing. “When you look under the lid, all they’re really offering is a solution for data residency and data localization, keeping data in country,” he says. “That’s part of sovereignty, but not all of sovereignty.”

In his experience, in-country data centers are the first thing organizations ask for to support data localization and data residency, but they also require enhanced controls over identity and access management. That’s critical because data sovereignty is as much about who has access to the data and why, as where it lives.

“It’s really important the only people who touch my data in what is supposedly a sovereign cloud environment are those I give permission to,” he adds. “Because it’s my data, and I’m the only one who can give the authority to grant access to it. That also applies to support and admin staff.”

Companies want control through where they store data but also to restrict how users can interact with it that might expose that information outside an approved environment or jurisdiction, adds Acceldata SVP Ali Afsar.

Access and control

Don’t confuse the regulatory requirements of data residency with data sovereignty, Scality CMO Paul Speciale warns. “Residency is about geography,” he says. “Sovereignty is about control, jurisdiction, and who ultimately has the legal authority to access data.”

For CIOs, the question is no longer simply where the data is but who can access it, who controls the encryption keys, under which legal framework it operates, and can that control be proven. That includes being able to show who accesses data, from where, and for what purpose, which requires verifiable controls like jurisdiction-aware data placement, immutable backups, tightly governed admin access, and clear audit trails.

The UK government’s recent call for evidence on the impact of international data flows on sovereignty makes this explicit, referring to transfer by access where personal data remains in the UK but is accessed from overseas, including by a user located in another country. Access transfers include administrative access, backups, disaster recovery, support incidents and sometimes — depending on the specific regulations — processing the data.

GDPR doesn’t mean data has to stay in the EU but it does require data to be protected to EU standards wherever it goes. Data transfer obligations for other jurisdictions can be far more restrictive, so multinational organizations may need access controls limiting who can see what regulated data from different locations.

RBI-regulated payment-system data, for instance, must be stored in India, but can be processed outside India, Afsar explains, as long as it’s deleted from overseas systems within 24 hours. And with limited exceptions, personal data in Saudi Arabia must be processed within the Kingdom, and China treats overseas access to some categories of data stored in China as a cross-border data activity. Russian laws require similar strict data localization, and personal data of Russian citizens has to be stored, processed, and kept within the country’s borders at all times, which is why LinkedIn was blocked there.

Elsewhere, regulations are most restrictive for specific markets like healthcare, financial, and public services. Not everything needs to be transferred to a sovereign cloud, Nasir points out, as use of that data is subject to regulatory compliance, and the increasing need for AI training.

“This is the data that’s going to have catastrophic business impacts if leaked,” he says. “To give enhanced controls and security for that data, you’d consider wrapping sovereign controls around it. Everything else not subject to compliance nor sensitive data can be accessed by whomever you want and from wherever.”

Sovereignty and safety

Organizations typically know data sovereignty rules well but still experience incidents like data breaches, government data access requests, and unauthorized cross-border transfers caused by, for example, traveling employees or excessive admin access, according to Kiteworks’ 2026 Data Security and Compliance Risk report.

“Location only tells a regulator where the data rests, not who can still reach it,” says Kiteworks’ EMEA GM Dario Perfettibile. “Every real exposure we’ve seen so far happens through access not geography.”

Thinking data needs to stay in region because then it’s safe gives a false sense of security if practiced as a substitute for proper data management. Access, data labelling, and retention polices take more work but are what can prevent incidents. “If you have a data policy in place, it can force a reapproval of the access,” he adds. “It can restrict access to you only, or it can block you out immediately.”

Location isn’t everything

Using a service closer to home doesn’t automatically make any of that easier. “Many organizations still assume sovereignty can be achieved by moving data from one cloud provider to another, or by replacing one hyperscaler with another,” says Keepit Group CISO Kim Larsen. “That misses the bigger picture.” CIOs should treat sovereignty as an operational capability not a compliance exercise, he adds, since sovereignty isn’t about scale or ownership of infrastructure for its own sake, but maintaining control.

“If an organization doesn’t know who can access its data, which legal frameworks govern that access, or whether it can recover its data independently, simply changing where the servers are located does little to reduce risk,” he says.

Just because something is based in your region doesn’t automatically make it a good choice. The EC, for instance, has set up accounts on W Social, an independent social media platform based on the AT protocol designed for data mobility and user migration, which Bluesky uses but is hosted in Europe.

The Commission’s own open source strategy suggests open source promises more control over digital infrastructure by avoiding vendor lock in, and a recent policy brief positions digital sovereignty as a form of digital independence. But having servers in the EU isn’t the same as freedom of digital movement since unlike Eurosky, based in Europe and using the same protocol, W limits interoperability so it can require identity verification, and has closed its source code after security researchers pointed out vulnerabilities.

Most organizations will continue to use both global and local providers, though they might prioritize what Nasir called glocal options built on partnerships between the two. “Organizations want to use a mixture of local and global providers,” he says. “They want all the innovation capabilities that the Microsofts, AWSs, and Googles of the world give us, that they consider local providers can’t match.”

IDC figures suggest only 4% of European organizations plan to switch to purely local options. “We can’t live without US technology today and there’s no appetite to do that,” says Nasir. Availability matters and local providers may not have the same level of infrastructure as global options. They can offer low hanging fruit like video conferencing solutions, but not more complicated directory and database services, or productivity software that’s intertwined with those US-provided services.

Choices about where to store data, and the technical controls to enforce that, have their own operational implications.

“Redundancy and resiliency are key tenets of sovereignty,” he adds. “You want to make sure your operations are always available. In order to enable that, you want to spread the risk.”

item.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio
item.description:
Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment.

By Sergio De Simone

item.title: The agents nobody meant to build
item.description:
This summer, our big concern as IT leaders was figuring out how to drive adoption and ROI for our AI purchases while keeping shadow AI at bay. My advice then: Give people transparent, sanctioned tools and put in place operational discipline to ensure the right tools are being deployed at the right times and in the right places. That advice still holds up.

But once again, the market shifted. Now, even the sanctioned tools are part of the problem, as we speed towards the autonomous, agentic enterprise.

Fortune reported recently that CIOs are “racing to put guardrails” around agents that one security chief called “a new kind of insider.” Gartner forecasts that 40% of enterprise applications will carry task-specific agents by the end of this year, up from under 5% last year. In the very same report, Gartner also predicts that 40% of enterprises will have to demote or shut down agents by 2027.

We’re building agents faster than we’re learning how to govern them.

Most leaders point to this as a visibility problem. We need to be able to see all the agents running and assign ownership to them. Fair points, but they only reveal the tip of the iceberg. The agents I’m concerned with are the ones nobody knows they’re creating.

Classic shadow AI is a tool someone chose: an employee connects a hyped consumer product straight into a corporate system, and now you have an unsanctioned agent running on unsanctioned software. That’s the fix I have written about before: give people a sanctioned version good enough that they don’t need the workaround.

The harder case is when an employee schedules a recurring job with their sanctioned AI desktop harness. Perhaps they schedule an agent to scan their email at set times, draft replies that they can send later, maybe even grant approvals on some minor things like direct report PTO requests. 

There’s nothing shadowy about the process. It’s working within a fully sanctioned tool that is being used exactly as licensed. But that employee just built an agent. And most people aren’t calling it that.

For the use cases described above, that’s a productivity tool for a specific employee. If their computer is off or the employee leaves the company and this de facto agent doesn’t run, nothing happens. But what happens if the employee builds a process that reads emails from a shared inbox and updates the ERP based on these emails? Now you have an agent that is part of the back-office automation of the company, and if this employee is off, a potentially critical process is not working. There is also an attack surface that nobody with a security mindset is aware of, a malicious email read by the agent might cause data corruption in the ERP, for example.

The problem is, there’s no owner to name and no approval to audit, because we’re not looking for that as an agent to name and label. You can’t put something on an inventory you don’t know exists. That’s a different failure mode than shadow IT, and it needs a different fix than a better registry.

This is where we begin to see the full depth and breadth of the iceberg we’re dealing with. It opens up entirely new considerations for our governance practices as well. We used to be most concerned with the browser and what employees could be inviting into our networks that way. The bigger concern now with agents is the security of the desktop itself, because that’s where they’re actually built and run. The way to mitigate it centers on two things: placing hard limits on what any of it can actually touch, and educating employees on what they’re actually doing, at the moment they’re most likely to do it.

Finding the balance point between control and innovation

Here’s where we also come up against the push and pull dynamic that rules our world as IT leaders, especially in the age of AI. Sometimes it seems like we have just two options: We can lock down the enterprise and hinder productivity and creativity for our employees, or we can make things easy for our employees and put our enterprise security at risk.

The first rule I go by here is embracing the chaos and discomfort. We don’t have this all figured out yet and that’s okay. Where I see my peers fail is when they try to force a process into place in these situations. You end up pushing the behavior you’re trying to manage outside of your area of control, making your employees even more likely to turn to unsafe workarounds.

The better approach is to put in place guardrails that allow your employees some space to experiment but limit the risk. This allows you to have some control while also being able to observe the actions your employees take, and reach out to move local processes to the corporate level.

For example, you can put in place controls directly into systems like CRM or ITSM or the MCPs used to interact with them. For example, make them read-only by default, and put in place rate limits at a more “human level”: a few hundred records a day, not the few hundred thousand that AI can process. Limit the fields and tables that can be edited, and rate limit them as well.

Then, if an agent misbehaves, whether due to malicious instructions or just a human guidance mistake, you catch the issue after a few dozen records get overwritten, rather than a thousand and retrace your steps to rebuild the files. You’re protected whether an agent is part of a central agent registry or not.

Governance is a literacy problem now, not a policy one

The other half of this has to educate the employees and designated power users, which we call AI Champions that are proxies of the CIO office in the various departments. You need to provide guidance the moment someone starts using it, not filed away in a policy no one reads. Every employee who gets a license for a sanctioned agentic tool at WalkMe takes a short course in basic agent concepts before their license activates.

Most organizations try to launch a full corporate AI training program, where research shows that only about a third of what employees learn is still being used a year later. The training fails because it teaches AI in the abstract, disconnected from the moment someone actually sits down to use it. Gate your training to the access itself, and it lands in the moment it’s most relevant.

The goal in the training isn’t to turn every employee into a developer. That’s not realistic, and I don’t think it’s the right goal either. What you’re aiming for is an understanding of what AI tool to use when: do you need a full-blown agent or just an agentic workflow, or maybe just good old deterministic integration, and the advantages, risks and limitations for each. They walk away knowing what an agent looks and acts like in the moment it’s most relevant, not months later when it’s done something they didn’t intend or expect.

Put those two fixes together and you’re solving a different problem than the one most governance conversations are stuck on. You don’t need a complete agent inventory to navigate this. You need defaults that are forgiving, and employees who recognize the moment they’ve crossed from using a tool to operating one.

AI didn’t just hand every employee a better tool this year. It handed a lot of them some of the responsibilities that used to belong to IT alone. Our job isn’t pretending that didn’t happen, or trying to claw it back. It’s making sure nobody has to become an IT admin to carry that responsibility safely.
